title: Data Drift & Decision Intelligence System
tagline: Detects data drift before your model silently degrades.
summary: An ML monitoring pipeline that flags when production data drifts from training data. PSI and KS-tests detect feature-level shifts, model performance is tracked across time windows, and an automated markdown report recommends retrain-or-monitor actions. Built as reusable Python modules consumed by five ordered notebooks following the CRISP-DM flow.

caseStudy.problem: Production machine learning models degrade silently. The data they were trained on stops matching reality as customers, markets, and seasons change, so predictions drift off before anyone notices. Most teams only find out after the model is already wrong in production. This project tackles the monitoring half of that problem: detect when the distribution of incoming data has shifted, work out whether that shift is actually hurting the model, and tell a non-technical stakeholder what to do about it.
requirements: Detect feature distribution drift with statistical tests (PSI, KS-test, chi-square)
Quantify the impact of drift on model performance across time windows
Identify which features actually drifted, not just that something changed
Produce an executive report with prioritized recommendations: retrain now or keep monitoring
Split training and test data chronologically so evaluation reflects deployment reality
Keep the drift layer model-agnostic so any trained model can be monitored
caseStudy.solution:
A Python package and five ordered notebooks that run an end-to-end monitoring drill on a synthetic dataset with gradual drift. Notebook 01 generates and validates the data, 02 engineers features, 03 trains a baseline Random Forest classifier on a chronological split, 04 runs PSI and KS-tests on every feature comparing the baseline window with a current window, and 05 monitors model performance across windows and writes a markdown executive report that connects drift to degradation and recommends actions.

The reusable modules are the real product. Drift detection, data validation, metrics, model training, and impact analysis are plain Python functions and classes in src/, so the notebook layer is thin. The README makes the swap clear: replace the synthetic data source and the baseline model, and notebooks 04 and 05 keep working unchanged because they never hard-code a model.

architecture.description:
Data moves through the pipeline in notebook order, and each notebook calls into the reusable modules. The EDA notebook generates and validates the dataset; feature engineering prepares the splits; the model trainer fits a baseline Random Forest on the earlier 80% of the timeline; drift detection compares the baseline distribution with the current one feature by feature; and impact analysis compares model metrics between consecutive time windows. The final notebook aggregates everything into reports/drift_report.md, the single deliverable an executive reads.

There is no service, API, or scheduler: the pipeline is designed to be executed in Jupyter and its outputs written to disk. That keeps it reproducible and simple, but monitoring is manual, not continuous.

caseStudy.implementation:
Drift detection is the core. Population Stability Index buckets both distributions into ten bins derived from the combined range, normalizes to percentages, and sums the standard formula; empty bins are smoothed with a small epsilon so log(0) never happens. Results are interpreted against standard thresholds: under 0.10 no drift, 0.10-0.25 small drift, over 0.25 significant. The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test adds a p-value at alpha 0.05, and categorical features get a chi-square test. The DriftDetector iterates every column and returns a per-feature dictionary with both statistics and their plain-language interpretations, plus a summary of how many features drifted.

The modeling layer refuses to leak the future: TimeAwareModelTrainer splits by row position (first 80% train, last 20% test) instead of a random shuffle, which is the correct stance for any monitoring story. The monitor compares consecutive windows, computes absolute and relative changes for accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC, and flags any metric that dropped more than 5%. The final notebook reads the drift summary and the performance comparison and emits an executive markdown report with an urgency framing, a per-feature table, and prioritized HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW actions. Everything is deterministic: a fixed random seed and a documented threshold table keep runs comparable.

challenges.title: log(0) inside the PSI formula when a bucket is empty
challenges.resolution: A small epsilon is added to both percentages before summing, so empty buckets contribute a bounded value instead of crashing.

challenges.title: Baseline and current windows have different sizes and ranges
challenges.resolution: Bins are derived from the combined min-max range and counts are normalized to percentages before comparison.

challenges.title: Random train/test splits leak the future into the model
challenges.resolution: Replaced them with a chronological split (first 80% train, last 20% test) so evaluation matches how the model would actually be used.

challenges.title: Categorical features have no natural binning for PSI
challenges.resolution: Handled with a chi-square test over normalized category frequencies instead.

challenges.title: Interpreting a raw PSI or KS number is not actionable
challenges.resolution: Every statistic is paired with a plain-language interpretation and a documented threshold table in the README.

lessons: The statistical methods are sound and genuinely reusable, but nothing in the repo proves the end-to-end run: every notebook is unexecuted, and models/ and reports/ are empty, so the drift report the README promises has never been committed.
A notebook-driven pipeline is fine for exploration, but production monitoring needs a scheduled job, an API, and alerting; none of those exist here.
Time-aware splits are the right instinct and should stay; a random split would have given falsely optimistic confidence in the baseline.
The dataset is synthetic and generated, so the PSI and degradation thresholds are untested against a real production corpus; thresholds are a starting point, not a finding.

The README overclaims: it calls this a production-grade platform, but it is a well-structured methodology project with no executed outputs, deployment, or tests. The honest next step is to run it and commit the artifacts.
future: Execute and commit the notebooks so the drift report, model metrics, and figures become reproducible artifacts in the repo.
Add a scheduled or CI-triggered runner so monitoring is continuous instead of manual notebook execution.
Add unit tests for PSI edge cases (identical distributions, empty buckets), KS on identical samples, and the degradation thresholds.
Connect to real production data through a model registry and a streaming source instead of a synthetic generator.
Add alerting (email or webhook) driven by the drift summary so a shift triggers action without a human opening a notebook.
